newsitem.title: FRANCE: French mini-budget to adjust 1996 spending - paper.
newsitem.headline: French mini-budget to adjust 1996 spending - paper.

text.p: The French government will present a revised 1996 budget on Wednesday which will fix this year's central government budget deficit at 287.9 billion francs compared with 287.8 billion originally forecast, financial daily Les Echos said.
The budget was to be presented to the cabinet later on Wednesday morning, followed by a 1030 GMT news conference by government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.

Les Echos said the mini-budget, traditionally presented towards the end of each year to keep spending plans on course, would make adjustments to allow for new spending on some areas by cutting spending elsewhere.
It would allow for some 23 billion francs in additional spending.

This would cover 4.5 billion in extra spending on housing susbidies to those on low incomes, the cost of a car buying incentive scheme which expired at the end of September, subsidies to state railways SNCF and Paris rail network RATP, and military operations abroad.
The mini-budget would also take account of a shortfall in net tax receipts, seen at some 23 billion francs less than expected, Les Echos said.
This would be offset by a rise in non-tax receipts, helped by contributions from state export credit agency Coface.
France's contribution to the European Union budget, which is subtracted from the revenue side of the government budget, would also be 7.8 billion francs less than expected, it said.
France would save another six billion francs on debt service charges, thanks to the recent fall in interest rates.
The mini-budget would allow for new spending cuts of 12.9 billion francs, on top of 15 billion francs in spending plans cancelled since the beginning of the year.
It would take account of an increase in plans for capital injections for state-owned companies. The budget originally allowed for capital injections of 16.5 billion francs.

It said the government had decided to delay until later payment of a two billion franc telephone bill to France Telecom, despite criticism of the delay made by the national accounts commission, the Cour des Comptes.
